title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 848–851 (Night 192, continuing nights-191), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 192 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The prince weeps and recites six lines on the girl whose glance bewitches. The vizier then counsels King Shahramān: he cannot sit by his son forever while the army goes unseen and the kingdom's order frays; let him move the prince to the palace in the royal grounds that stands out in the sea, hold court there on Mondays and Thursdays, and stay with his son the rest of the week, and he caps the advice with three lines on trusting fortune too far. The king agrees. The sea palace is described — reached by a causeway twenty cubits wide, its floor of coloured marble, its ceiling painted and inlaid with gold and lapis — and Qamar al-Zamān is set there on a throne of juniper wood, but he wastes away with love, neither eating nor sleeping, while his father sits at his head and receives the court twice a week. The story turns to the Lady Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands and the seven palaces: the jinn had laid her back in her own bed, and at dawn she wakes, finds the young man gone from her arms and screams. Her women run in; she demands of the chief stewardess where her beloved is, the handsome youth who slept beside her all night. The old woman, terrified, swears she has seen no young man and begs her to stop a jest that could cost them all their lives if it reached her father, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالتِّسْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-tisʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninety-second night,
sentences.n: al-thāniya, “the second”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-tisʿūna, “and the ninety”, and baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”, as in the nights before. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا أَنْشَدَ لِأَبِيهِ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ بَكَى وَاشْتَكَى وَتَأَوَّهَ مِنْ كَبِدٍ مَجْرُوحٍ وَأَنْشَدَ أَيْضًا هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā anshada li-abīhi hādhihi al-abyāta bakā wa-ishtakā wa-taʾawwaha min kabidin majrūḥin wa-anshada ayḍan hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-recited to-his-father these the-verses, wept and-complained and-groaned from a-liver wounded, and-recited also these the-verses:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān had recited those verses to his father, he wept and lamented and groaned from a wounded heart, and recited these verses as well:
sentences.n: Last night broke off just as he began to recite; the verses themselves are never given, and Shahrazād takes up the story after them. bakā wa-ishtakā, “wept and complained”, a rhyming pair. taʾawwaha, Form V, “to say āh, to groan”; its shadda is printed. The kabid, “liver”, is in Arabic a seat of grief and passion, as the heart is in English. kabid is usually feminine, but majrūḥ, “wounded”, is left masculine here. ayḍan, “also”.

sentences.t:
خُذُوا حِذْرَكُمْ مِنْ طَرْفِهَا فَهْوَ سَاحِرٌ * وَلَيْسَ بِنَاجٍ مَنْ رَمَتْهُ الْمَحَاجِرُ
وَلَا تَخْدَعُوا مِنْ رِقَّةٍ فِي كَلَامِهَا * فَاِنَّ الْحُمَيَّا لِلْعُقُولِ تُخَامِرُ
مُنَعَّمَةٌ لَوْ لَامَسَ الْوَرْدُ خَدَّهَا * بَكَتْ وَجَرَتْ مِنْ مُقْلَتَيْهِ الْمَوَاطِرُ
فَلَوْ فِي الْكَرَى مَرَّ النَّسِيمُ بِاَرْضِهَا * سَرَى اَبَدًا مِنْ اَرْضِهَا وَهْوَ عَاطِرُ
قَلَائِدُهَا تَشْكُو رَنِينَ وِشَاحِهَا * وَقَدْ خَرَّسَتْ مِنْ مِعْصَمَيْهَا الْاَسَاوِرُ
عَذُولِي لَحَاكَ اللّٰهُ مَا اَنْتَ مُنْصِفُ * فَعَنْ حُسْنِ هٰذَا الظَّبْيِ تُثْنَى النَّوَاظِرُ
sentences.tr:
khudhū ḥidhrakum min ṭarfihā fa-hwa sāḥirun * wa-laysa bi-nājin man ramathu al-maḥājiru
wa-lā takhdaʿū min riqqatin fī kalāmihā * fa-inna al-ḥumayyā li-al-ʿuqūli tukhāmiru
munaʿʿamatun law lāmasa al-wardu khaddahā * bakat wa-jarat min muqlatayhi al-mawāṭiru
fa-law fī al-karā marra al-nasīmu bi-arḍihā * sarā abadan min arḍihā wa-hwa ʿāṭiru
qalāʾiduhā tashkū ranīna wishāḥihā * wa-qad kharrasat min miʿṣamayhā al-asāwiru
ʿadhūlī laḥāka Allāhu mā anta munṣifu * fa-ʿan ḥusni hādhā al-ẓabyi tuthnā al-nawāẓiru
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; as usual it writes the hamza of words like اِنَّ, اَرْض, اَبَدًا, الْاَسَاوِر and اَنْتَ as a vowel on bare alif, and shortens huwa to hwa (فَهْوَ, وَهْوَ) for the metre. al-maḥājir, “the hollows of the eyes”, for the eyes themselves: the glance shoots like an archer. wa-lā takhdaʿū is printed with the active vowels, “do not deceive”; the sense wants the passive, lā tukhdaʿū, “do not be deceived”, which the same letters allow, and the translation follows the sense. al-ḥumayyā, “wine”, properly the first fierce rush of it; khāmara, Form III, “to steal into, take hold of”, of wine on the mind, from the root of khamr. munaʿʿama, Form II passive participle, “delicately reared”. min muqlatayhi, “from its (his) two eyes”: the suffix is masculine, so while she weeps at the touch, the rains pour from the rose’s own eyes, as if it grieved at having touched her; it may be a slip for muqlatayhā, “her eyes”, which scans the same, but the print is kept. al-mawāṭir, “the rains”, tears. In the fourth line the breeze takes her fragrance and keeps it for ever. The wishāḥ is a jewelled band worn across the body: her waist is slender, so it swings and rings; her wrists are full, so the bracelets cannot move or sound. The necklaces “complain” of the din. kharrasat, Form II, is printed with the shadda the metre needs; the common verb for “to be dumb” is kharisa, Form I. laḥāka Allāhu, “may God strip you” (as bark from a stick), a curse on the ʿadhūl, the reproacher, the stock figure who blames the lover. mā anta munṣifu: after mā Classical usage puts the predicate in the accusative, munṣifan; the print has munṣifu. tuthnā, passive, “are turned back”, dazzled.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ الْوَزِيرُ لِلْمَلِكِ يَا مَلِكَ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَوَانِ إِلَى مَتَي أَنْتَ تَقْعُدُ عِنْدَ وَلَدِكَ وَأَنْتَ مَحْجُوبٌ عَنِ الْعَسَاكِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla al-wazīru li-al-maliki yā malika al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni ilā matā anta taqʿudu ʿinda waladika wa-anta maḥjūbun ʿani al-ʿasākiri
sentences.l: And-when he-finished from his-poetry, said the-vizier to-the-king: O king (of) the-age and-the-time, until when you sit with your-son, and-you (are) veiled from the-troops?
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, the vizier said to the king, “King of the age and of the time, how long will you sit by your son, hidden away from your troops?
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”. malik al-ʿaṣr wa-al-awān, “king of the age and the time”, a courtly address. The print spells matā, “when”, with a dotted ي, متي, where ى is usual; ilā matā, “until when”, how long. maḥjūb, “veiled, screened off”, the word for a ruler who keeps himself from his people; wa-anta maḥjūbun …, “while you are …”, a circumstantial clause. ʿasākir, plural of ʿaskar, “army, troops”.

sentences.t: فَرُبَّمَا يَنْفَسِدُ عَلَيْكَ نِظَامُ مَمْلَكَتِكَ بِسَبَبِ بُعْدِكَ عَنْ أَرْبَابِ دَوْلَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-rubbamā yanfasidu ʿalayka niẓāmu mamlakatika bi-sababi buʿdika ʿan arbābi dawlatika
sentences.l: For-perhaps becomes-spoiled upon-you (the) order (of) your-kingdom by-cause (of) your-distance from (the) lords (of) your-state.
sentences.i: It may well be that the order of your kingdom will fall apart on you, because you keep yourself far from the great men of your state.
sentences.n: rubbamā, “perhaps, it may be”; its shadda is printed. yanfasidu, Form VII of fasada, “to go bad, fall into disorder”, a Middle Arabic form beside Classical yafsudu; ʿalayka, “on you”, to your cost. bi-sababi, “by reason of”. arbāb al-dawla, “the lords of the state”, the high officers of government.

sentences.t: وَالْعَاقِلُ إِذَا كَانَ بِجِسْمِهِ جِرَاحَاتٌ مُخْتَلِفَاتٌ فَلْيُدَاوِي الْأَخْطَرَ مِنْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-al-ʿāqilu idhā kāna bi-jismihi jirāḥātun mukhtalifātun fa-l-yudāwī al-akhṭara minhā
sentences.l: And-the-sensible-one, if there-were in-his-body wounds various, then-let-him-treat the-most-dangerous of-them.
sentences.i: A sensible man with wounds of different kinds on his body should treat the most dangerous of them first.
sentences.n: bi-jismihi, bi- “in, on”. kāna stays masculine before its feminine plural subject jirāḥāt, as a verb that comes first may. fa-l-yudāwī, “let him treat”: li- of command, its vowel lost after fa-. Classical grammar wants the jussive, fa-l-yudāwi, without the long ī; the print keeps the ي, a common Middle Arabic form. al-akhṭar, “the most dangerous”, elative of khaṭīr. The moral is plain: the kingdom is the graver wound.

sentences.t: وَالرَّأْيُ عِنْدِي أَنْ تَنْقُلَ وَلَدَكَ مِنْ هٰذَا الْمَكَانِ إِلَى الْقَصْرِ الَّذِي فِى السَّرَايَةِ الْمُطِلِّ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ وَتَنْقَطِعَ عِنْدَ وَلَدِكَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-raʾyu ʿindī an tanqula waladaka min hādhā al-makāni ilā al-qaṣri alladhī fī al-sarāyati al-muṭilli ʿalā al-baḥri wa-tanqaṭiʿa ʿinda waladika fīhi
sentences.l: And-the-opinion with-me (is) that you-move your-son from this the-place to the-palace which (is) in the-saray, the-overlooking upon the-sea, and-you-cut-yourself-off with your-son in-it,
sentences.i: My counsel is that you move your son from this place to the palace in the seraglio that looks out over the sea, and shut yourself away there with your son;
sentences.n: The print has والدك, “your father”, a misprint for ولدك, “your son”, corrected here: the vizier is urging the king to stay with his son, as he says again a few words on. The hamza of الرأي is printed. al-sarāya, from Turkish saray, “palace”, here the royal compound; the print writes fī with ى, فى. al-muṭill, Form IV participle of aṭalla ʿalā, “to overlook”, agrees with al-qaṣr. tanqaṭiʿa, Form VII, “to withdraw, cut oneself off”; it and tanqula are subjunctive after an.

sentences.t: وَتَجْعَلَ لِلدِّيوَانِ وَالْمَوْكِبِ فِي كُلِّ جُمْعَةٍ يَوْمَيْنِ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ وَيَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-tajʿala li-al-dīwāni wa-al-mawkibi fī kulli jumʿatin yawmayni yawma al-khamīsi wa-yawma al-ithnayni
sentences.l: and-you-make for-the-council and-the-procession in every week two-days: (the) day (of) the-Thursday and-(the)-day (of) the-Monday;
sentences.i: and that you set aside two days in every week for the council and the audience, Thursday and Monday.
sentences.n: jaʿala li-, “to set aside for”: li- marks what the days are for. tajʿala is still governed by an. dīwān, the council where the ruler hears business; mawkib, his formal public appearance, the procession and audience. jumʿa, “Friday”, and so “week”. yawmayni, dual accusative, then spelled out as the two named days: al-khamīs, “the fifth”, Thursday, and al-ithnayn, “the two”, the second day, Monday.

sentences.t: فَيَدْخُلُ عَلَيْكَ فِيهِمَا الْأُمَرَاءُ وَالْوُزَرَاءُ وَالْحُجَّابُ وَالنُّوَّابُ وَأَرْبَابُ الدَّوْلَةِ وَخَوَاصُّ الْمَمْلَكَةِ وَبَقِيَّةُ الْعَسْكَرِ وَالرَّعِيَّةُ وَيَعْرِضُونَ عَلَيْكَ أَحْوَالَهُمْ فَتَقْضِي لَهُمْ حَوَائِجَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-yadkhulu ʿalayka fīhimā al-umarāʾu wa-al-wuzarāʾu wa-al-ḥujjābu wa-al-nuwwābu wa-arbābu al-dawlati wa-khawāṣṣu al-mamlakati wa-baqiyyatu al-ʿaskari wa-al-raʿiyyatu wa-yaʿriḍūna ʿalayka aḥwālahum fa-taqḍī lahum ḥawāʾijahum
sentences.l: So-enter upon-you in-them-two the-emirs and-the-viziers and-the-chamberlains and-the-deputies and-(the)-lords (of) the-state and-(the)-elite (of) the-kingdom and-(the)-rest (of) the-army and-the-subjects, and-they-lay-before you their-conditions, and-you-settle for-them their-needs;
sentences.i: Then on those days the emirs and viziers, the chamberlains and deputies, the lords of the state and the chief men of the kingdom, the rest of the army and the common people will come in to you and lay their affairs before you, and you will see to their needs.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to come in to (someone)”, into his presence. The singular yadkhulu stands before a long string of plural subjects, as a verb that leads may. ḥājib, “chamberlain”, the officer who governs access to the ruler; nāʾib, “deputy”; the shaddas of الحجّاب and النوّاب are printed. khawāṣṣ, “the elite, the intimates”. al-raʿiyya, “the flock”, a ruler’s subjects. ʿaraḍa ʿalā, “to lay before”. qaḍā ḥājatan, “to fulfil a need”, with li- for the one served. The hamza of حوائجهم is printed.

sentences.t: وَاحْكُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ وَخُذْ وَأَعْطِ مَعَهُمْ وَأْمُرْ وَانْهِ بَيْنَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-uḥkum baynahum wa-khudh wa-aʿṭi maʿahum wa-ʾmur wa-inhi baynahum
sentences.l: And-judge between-them, and-take and-give with-them, and-command and-forbid among-them;
sentences.i: Judge between them, deal with them in give and take, command and forbid among them;
sentences.n: The vizier slips from the subjunctive into plain commands. khudh wa-aʿṭi maʿa, “take and give with”, to have dealings with people. amara and nahā, “to command” and “to forbid”, the stock pair for ruling. The print writes the hamza of وأمر, so wa-ʾmur keeps the root’s hamza; the kasra of وانهِ is printed too: inhi, the imperative of nahā, which drops its final letter.

sentences.t: وَبَقِيَّةَ الْجُمْعَةِ تَكُونُ عِنْدَ وَلَدِكَ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ حَتَّى يُفَرِّجَ اللَّهُ عَنْكَ وَعَنْهُ
sentences.tr: wa-baqiyyata al-jumʿati takūnu ʿinda waladika Qamari al-Zamāni wa-lam tazal ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati ḥattā yufarrija Allāhu ʿanka wa-ʿanhu
sentences.l: and-(the)-rest (of) the-week you-are with your-son Qamar al-Zamān; and-not you-ceased upon that the-state until relieves God from-you and-from-him.
sentences.i: and for the rest of the week you will be with your son Qamar al-Zamān. Keep on in this way until God brings relief to you and to him.
sentences.n: baqiyyata al-jumʿati, accusative of time, “for the rest of the week”. lam tazal, “you did not cease”, is a past form, but here it means “keep on, stay”: the text uses lam yazal loosely for lasting in a state. farraja ʿan, Form II, “to bring relief to”: ʿan marks the one set free, as in the last night.

sentences.t: وَلَاتَأْمَنْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ مِنْ نَوَائِبِ الزَّمَانِ وَطَوَارِقِ الْحَدَثَانِ فَإِنَّ الْعَاقِلَ دَائِمًا مُحَاذِرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lā taʾman ayyuhā al-maliku min nawāʾibi al-zamāni wa-ṭawāriqi al-ḥadathāni fa-inna al-ʿāqila dāʾiman muḥādhirun
sentences.l: And-not feel-safe, O the-king, from (the) calamities (of) the-time and-(the)-night-knockers (of) the-events; for-indeed the-sensible-one (is) always wary.
sentences.i: And do not feel secure, O king, against the blows of fortune and the sudden strokes of chance; for the wise man is always on his guard.
sentences.n: The print sets ولا and تأمن together, ولاتأمن; the spacing is kept. lā taʾman, prohibition with the jussive; amina min, “to feel safe from”. nawāʾib, “calamities”, and ṭawāriq, “things that come knocking by night”, so sudden misfortunes; zamān and ḥadathān, “time” and “the run of events”, rhyme. muḥādhir, Form III participle, “wary, on guard”. The hamza of تأمن, نوائب and دائما is printed.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aḥsana qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: And-what made-fine (the) saying (of) the-poet!
sentences.i: How well the poet put it:
sentences.n: mā aḥsana …, the exclamation of wonder: the verb aḥsana in a fixed form, its object, qawla, in the accusative.

sentences.t:
حَسَّنْتَ ظَنَّكَ بِالْاَيَّامِ اِذْ حَسُنَتْ * وَلَمْ تَخَفْ سُوْءَ مَا يَأْتِي بِهِ الْقَدَرُ
وَسَالَمَتْكَ اللَّيَالِي فَاغْتَرَرْتَ بِهَا * وَعِنْدَ صَفْوِ اللَّيَالِي يَحْدُثُ الْكَدَرُ
يَا مَعْشَرَ النَّاسِ مَنْ كَانَ الزَّمَانُ لَهُ * مُسَاعِدًا فَلْيَكُنْ مِنْ رَأْيه الحَذَرُ
sentences.tr:
ḥassanta ẓannaka bi-al-ayyāmi idh ḥasunat * wa-lam takhaf sūʾa mā yaʾtī bihi al-qadaru
wa-sālamatka al-layālī fa-ightararta bihā * wa-ʿinda ṣafwi al-layālī yaḥduthu al-kadaru
yā maʿshara al-nāsi man kāna al-zamānu lahu * musāʿidan fa-l-yakun min raʾyihi al-ḥadharu
sentences.n: The print points the verse, and its pointing is kept; the final letter of رَأْيه is left bare there, and the word is raʾyihi, “his judgment”. ḥassana ẓannahu bi-, Form II, “to think well of”: bi- marks what one trusts. atā bi-, “to bring”: bi- marks the thing brought. sālama, Form III, “to make peace with”; ightarra bi-, Form VIII, “to be deceived by, trust wrongly in”. ṣafw and kadar, “clearness” and “muddiness” (of water), a stock pair for good times and bad. musāʿidan, the predicate of kāna, carried over into the second half-line. fa-l-yakun, li- of command with the jussive. The print sets a sukūn on the wāw of سُوْءَ and writes the hamza of اِذْ as a kasra on bare alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السُّلْطَانُ مِنَ الْوَزِيرِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ رَأٰهُ صَوَابًا وَنَصِيحَةً لَهُ فِي مَصْلَحَتِهِ فَأَثَّرَ عِنْدَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-sulṭānu mina al-wazīri hādhā al-kalāma raʾāhu ṣawāban wa-naṣīḥatan lahu fī maṣlaḥatihi fa-aththara ʿindahu
sentences.l: And-when heard the-sultan from the-vizier this the-speech, he-saw-it right and-counsel for-him in his-interest, and-it-made-an-impression with-him,
sentences.i: When the sultan heard these words from the vizier, he saw that they were right, good counsel for his own welfare, and they weighed with him;
sentences.n: raʾāhu, “he saw it (to be)”, with two objects, the pronoun and ṣawāban; the print writes رأه without the long alif, pointed here with a dagger alif; its hamza is printed. naṣīḥa, “sincere advice”; maṣlaḥa, “interest, welfare”. aththara ʿinda, Form II, “to make an impression on”.

sentences.t: وَخَافَ أَنْ يَنْفَسِدَ عَلَيْهِ نِظَامُ الْمُلْكِ فَنَهَضَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَأَمَرَ بِتَحْوِيلِ وَلَدِةِ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ إِلَى الْقَصْرِ الَّذِي فِى السَّرَايَةِ الْمُطِلِّ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-khāfa an yanfasida ʿalayhi niẓāmu al-mulki fa-nahaḍa min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-amara bi-taḥwīli waladihi min dhālika al-makāni ilā al-qaṣri alladhī fī al-sarāyati al-muṭilli ʿalā al-baḥri
sentences.l: and-he-feared that becomes-spoiled upon-him (the) order (of) the-kingship; so-he-rose from his-time and-his-hour and-commanded (the) moving (of) his-son from that the-place to the-palace which (is) in the-saray, the-overlooking upon the-sea.
sentences.i: he feared that the order of his realm would fall apart on him. So he rose then and there and ordered his son moved from that place to the palace in the seraglio that looks out over the sea.
sentences.n: The print has التصر, a misprint for القصر, “the palace”, corrected here: the words repeat the vizier’s. min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, at once. amara bi-, “to command”: the verb takes the thing ordered with bi-. taḥwīl, Form II verbal noun, “moving, transferring”. The print writes waladihi, “his son”, with ة for the pronoun, ولدة, one of its spelling habits.

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا الْقَصْرُ كَانَ فِي وَسَطِ الْبَحْرِ يَمْشُونَ إِلَيْهِ عَلَى مَمْشَاةٍ عَرْضُهَا عِشْرُونَ ذِرَاعًا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā al-qaṣru kāna fī wasaṭi al-baḥri yamshūna ilayhi ʿalā mamshātin ʿarḍuhā ʿishrūna dhirāʿan
sentences.l: And-this the-palace was in (the) middle (of) the-sea; they-walk to-it upon a-walkway, its-width (is) twenty cubits.
sentences.i: This palace stood in the middle of the sea, and people walked out to it on a causeway twenty cubits wide.
sentences.n: mamshāt, “walkway”, a place-noun from mashā, “to walk”, here a causeway over the water. ʿarḍuhā …, an unmarked relative clause after an indefinite noun. dhirāʿ, “cubit”, a forearm’s length; after ʿishrūna the counted noun is singular and accusative.

sentences.t: وَبِدَائِرِ الْقَصْرِ شَبَابِيكُ مُطِلَّةٌ عَلَى الْبَحْرِ وَأَرْضُهُ مَفْرُوشَةٌ بِالرُّخَامِ الْمُلَوَّنِ وَسَقْفُهُ مَدْهُونٌ بِأَنْوَاعِ الدِّهَانَاتِ وَأَفْخَرِهَا وَمَنْقُوشٌ بِالذَّهَبِ وَاللَّازَوَرْدِ
sentences.tr: wa-bi-dāʾiri al-qaṣri shabābīku muṭillatun ʿalā al-baḥri wa-arḍuhu mafrūshatun bi-al-rukhāmi al-mulawwani wa-saqfuhu madhūnun bi-anwāʿi al-dihānāti wa-afkharihā wa-manqūshun bi-al-dhahabi wa-al-lāzawardi
sentences.l: And-in-(the)-circuit (of) the-palace (were) windows overlooking upon the-sea; and-its-floor (was) spread with-the-marble the-coloured, and-its-ceiling painted with-(the)-kinds (of) the-paints and-(the)-finest-of-them, and-figured with-the-gold and-the-lapis-lazuli.
sentences.i: All round the palace were windows looking out over the sea; its floor was laid with coloured marble, and its ceiling was painted with every kind of paint, and the finest, and worked with gold and lapis lazuli.
sentences.n: bi-dāʾiri al-qaṣri, “all round the palace”: dāʾir, “circuit”, with bi- of place; its hamza is printed. shabābīk, “windows, lattices”, takes no tanwīn, as plurals of this pattern do not. The bi- after mafrūsha, madhūn and manqūsh marks the material: “laid with, painted with, worked with”. dihānāt, plural of dihān, “paint, varnish”. afkharihā, “the finest of them”, elative of fākhir, joined to anwāʿi. lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”, the blue stone and the pigment made from it.

sentences.t: فَفَرَشُوا لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فِيهِ الْفِرَاشَ الْحَرِيرَ الْفَاخِرَ وَالْبُسُطَ الْمُطَرَّزَ وَأَلْبَسُوا حِيطَانَهُ خَاصَّ الدِّيبَاجِ وَأَرْخَوْا عَلَيْهِ السِّتَارَاتِ الْمُكَلَّلَةَ بِالْجَوَاهِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-farashū li-Qamari al-Zamāni fīhi al-firāsha al-ḥarīra al-fākhira wa-al-busuṭa al-muṭarraza wa-albasū ḥīṭānahu khāṣṣa al-dībāji wa-arkhaw ʿalayhi al-sitārāti al-mukallalata bi-al-jawāhiri
sentences.l: So-they-spread for-Qamar al-Zamān in-it the-bedding, the-silk, the-splendid, and-the-carpets the-embroidered, and-they-clothed its-walls (with the) choicest (of) the-brocade, and-they-let-down over-it the-curtains the-crowned with-the-jewels.
sentences.i: There they spread for Qamar al-Zamān bedding of splendid silk and embroidered carpets, hung its walls with the choicest brocade, and let down over it curtains set with jewels.
sentences.n: The print has الديباح, a misprint for الديباج, “brocade”, corrected here. li-Qamari al-Zamāni, li- “for”. al-firāsh al-ḥarīr, “the bedding, the silk”: the material set beside the noun in apposition, “silk bedding”. busuṭ, plural of bisāṭ, “carpet”, takes a masculine singular adjective, al-muṭarraz, “embroidered”, a loose agreement of the text. albasa, Form IV, “to clothe”, takes two objects, the walls and what they are dressed in. khāṣṣ, “choice, select”. arkhā, Form IV, “to let hang down”. mukallal bi-, “crowned with, ringed with”, from iklīl, “crown, circlet”.

sentences.t: وَأَجْلَسُوا فِيهِ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى سَرِيرٍ مِنَ الْعَرْعَرِ مُكَلَّلٍ بِالدُّرِّ وَالْجَوْهَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-ajlasū fīhi Qamara al-Zamāni ʿalā sarīrin mina al-ʿarʿari mukallalin bi-al-durri wa-al-jawhari
sentences.l: And-they-seated in-it Qamar al-Zamān upon a-couch of the-juniper, crowned with-the-pearls and-the-gems.
sentences.i: And they seated Qamar al-Zamān there on a couch of juniper wood set with pearls and gems.
sentences.n: ajlasa, Form IV, “to make sit, seat”. sarīr, a raised couch or throne. ʿarʿar, “juniper”, a fragrant wood. durr, “large pearls”; its shadda is printed. jawhar, “gems”, a collective.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا أَنَّهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ اشْتِغَالِهِ بِالصَّبِيَّةِ وَعِشْقِهِ لَهَا تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنُهُ وَنَحَلَ جِسْمُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa Qamaru al-Zamāni ʿalayhi illā annahu min shiddati ishtighālihi bi-al-ṣabiyyati wa-ʿishqihi lahā taghayyara lawnuhu wa-naḥala jismuhu
sentences.l: So-sat Qamar al-Zamān upon-it; except that-he, from (the) intensity (of) his-preoccupation with-the-girl and-his-passion for-her, changed his-colour and-grew-thin his-body,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān sat on it; but so taken up was he with the girl, and so deep in love with her, that his colour changed and his body wasted,
sentences.n: illā anna, “except that, only”. ishtaghala bi-, Form VIII, “to be taken up with”: bi- marks what fills his mind. ʿishq, passionate love; li- marks the one loved. naḥala, “to grow thin, waste away”. The shaddas of الّا and الصبيّة are printed.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ لَا يَأْكُلُ وَلَايَشْرَبُ وَلَايَنَامُ وَصَارَ كَالْمَرِيضِ الَّذِي لَهُ عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً مَرِيضًا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra lā yaʾkulu wa-lā yashrabu wa-lā yanāmu wa-ṣāra ka-al-marīḍi alladhī lahu ʿishrūna sanatan marīḍan
sentences.l: and-he-came-to not eat and-not drink and-not sleep, and-he-became like-the-sick-one who (has) to-him twenty years sick.
sentences.i: and he would neither eat nor drink nor sleep, until he was like a man who has been sick for twenty years.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to come to (do)”, here “he took to not eating”. The print sets ولا together with the verb twice, ولايشرب, ولاينام; the spacing is kept. ka-, “like”. lahu ʿishrūna sanatan marīḍan, “who has twenty years, sick”, that is, who has been ill for twenty years; marīḍan is an accusative of state. The hamza of يأكل is printed.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ وَالِدُةُ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ وَحَزِنَ عَلَيْهِ حُزْنًا عَظِيمًا
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa wāliduhu ʿinda raʾsihi wa-ḥazina ʿalayhi ḥuznan ʿaẓīman
sentences.l: So-sat his-father at his-head and-grieved over-him a-grief great.
sentences.i: His father sat at his head and grieved over him deeply.
sentences.n: The print writes wāliduhu, “his father”, with ة for the pronoun, والدة. ḥazina ʿalā, “to grieve for”; ḥuznan ʿaẓīman, the verb’s own noun as object, to strengthen it. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ الْمَلِكُ فِي كُلِّ يَوْمِ اثْنَيْنِ وَيَوْمِ خَمِيسٍ يَأْذَنُ بِدُخُولِ الْأُمَرَاءِ وَالْحُجَّابِ وَالنُّوَّابِ وَأَرْبَابِ الدَّوْلَةِ وَالْعَسَاكِرِ وَالرَّعِيَّةِ فِي ذٰلِكَ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra al-maliku fī kulli yawmi ithnayni wa-yawmi khamīsin yaʾdhanu bi-dukhūli al-umarāʾi wa-al-ḥujjābi wa-al-nuwwābi wa-arbābi al-dawlati wa-al-ʿasākiri wa-al-raʿiyyati fī dhālika al-qaṣri
sentences.l: And-came the-king, in every day (of) Monday and-day (of) Thursday, to-permit (the) entry (of) the-emirs and-the-chamberlains and-the-deputies and-(the)-lords (of) the-state and-the-troops and-the-subjects in that the-palace;
sentences.i: Every Monday and Thursday the king would give leave for the emirs, chamberlains and deputies, the lords of the state, the troops and the common people to come into that palace,
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect again, here of a settled habit. adhina bi-, “to permit”: bi- marks what is allowed. yawm ithnayn, “a Monday”, and yawm khamīs, “a Thursday”, now without the article. The hamza of يأذن and the shaddas of الحجّاب and النوّاب are printed.

sentences.t: فَيَدْخُلُونَ عَلَيْهِ وَيُؤَدُّونَ وَظَائِفَ الْخِدْمَةِ وَيُقِيمُونَ عِنْدَةُ إِلَى آخِرِ النَّهَارِ ثُمَّ يَنْصَرِفُونَ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-yadkhulūna ʿalayhi wa-yuʾaddūna waẓāʾifa al-khidmati wa-yuqīmūna ʿindahu ilā ākhiri al-nahāri thumma yanṣarifūna ilā ḥāli sabīlihim
sentences.l: and-they-enter upon-him and-perform (the) duties (of) the-service and-stay with-him to (the) end (of) the-day; then they-go-off to (the) state (of) their-way.
sentences.i: and they would come in to him, perform the duties of their service and stay with him until the end of the day, and then go their ways.
sentences.n: addā, Form II, “to discharge, perform”; waẓāʾif al-khidma, “the duties of service”, the attendance owed to the ruler. The print writes ʿindahu with ة for the pronoun, عندة. inṣarafa ilā ḥāli sabīlihi, Form VII, “to go off on one’s way”, a set phrase. The hamza of ويؤدّون, وظائف and آخر is printed, and so is the shadda of ويؤدّون.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ يَدْخُلُ الْمَلِكُ عِنْدَ وَلَدِةِ فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَلَا يُفَارِقُهُ لَيْلًا وَلَا نَهَارًا
sentences.tr: thumma yadkhulu al-maliku ʿinda waladihi fī dhālika al-makāni wa-lā yufāriquhu laylan wa-lā nahāran
sentences.l: Then enters the-king with his-son in that the-place, and-not he-leaves-him by-night and-not by-day.
sentences.i: Then the king would go in to his son in that place, and never leave him, night or day.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿinda, “to go in to (someone)”, a looser turn beside dakhala ʿalā. waladihi is again printed with ة, ولدة. fāraqa, Form III, “to part from”. laylan wa-lā nahāran, accusatives of time.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ مُدَّةَ أَيَّامٍ وَلَيَالِي مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati muddata ayyāmin wa-layālī mina al-zamāni
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased upon that the-state (for a) period (of) days and-nights of the-time.
sentences.i: So he remained for a space of days and nights.
sentences.n: muddata, accusative of time, “for a period”. layālī, “nights”: Classical grammar has layālin here, the long ī dropped and the tanwīn added; the print keeps the ي, a usual Middle Arabic form.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ بْنِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri Qamari al-Zamāni ibni al-maliki Shahramāna
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair (of) Qamar al-Zamān, son (of) the-king Shahramān.
sentences.i: So much for Qamar al-Zamān, son of King Shahramān.
sentences.n: The storyteller’s formula for leaving one thread to take up another. ibn, “son”, is written without its alif between names. Shahramān takes no tanwīn, as a foreign proper name.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ الْغَيُورِ صَاحِبِ الْجَزَائِرِ وَالسَّبْعَةِ قُصُورٍ فَإِنَّ الْجِنَّ لَمَّا حَمَلُوهَا وَوَضَعُوهَا فِي فِرَاشِهَا لَمْ تَزَلْ نَائِمَةً إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-malikati Budūra binti al-maliki al-Ghayūri ṣāḥibi al-jazāʾiri wa-al-sabʿati quṣūrin fa-inna al-jinna lammā ḥamalūhā wa-waḍaʿūhā fī firāshihā lam tazal nāʾimatan ilā an ṭalaʿa al-fajru
sentences.l: And-as-for what was of (the) affair (of) the-queen Budūr, daughter (of) the-king al-Ghayūr, lord (of) the-islands and-the-seven palaces, then-indeed the-jinn, when they-carried-her and-placed-her in her-bed, not she-ceased sleeping until that rose the-dawn.
sentences.i: As for Queen Budūr, daughter of King al-Ghayūr, lord of the islands and the seven palaces: when the jinn had carried her back and laid her in her bed, she slept on until dawn broke.
sentences.n: wa-ammā … fa-, “as for …, then”, taking up the other thread. al-malika, “the queen”, used here of the princess. Budūr, “full moons”, takes no tanwīn as a woman’s name, so its genitive ends in -a. al-sabʿati quṣūrin, “the seven palaces”: Classical usage wants sabʿati al-quṣūri, with the article on the counted noun; the text puts it on the number, a colloquial turn. After fa-inna al-jinna the sentence changes course, as spoken narration does: “the jinn, when they had carried her … she slept on”. lam tazal, “she did not cease”, so “she went on”. The hamza of الجزائر and نائمة is printed.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبَهَتْ مِنْ مَنَامِهَا وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى حَيْلِهَا وَالْتَفَتَتْ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَلَمْ تَرَ الشَّابَّ الَّذِي كَانَ فِي حِضْنِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-intabahat min manāmihā wa-jalasat ʿalā ḥaylihā wa-iltafatat yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-lam tara al-shābba alladhī kāna fī ḥiḍnihā
sentences.l: Then-she-awoke from her-sleep and-sat upon her-strength and-turned right and-left, and-not she-saw the-youth who was in her-bosom.
sentences.i: Then she woke from her sleep, sat up and looked to right and left, and did not see the youth who had been in her arms.
sentences.n: intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake, become alert”. jalasa ʿalā ḥaylihi, colloquial, “to sit up”, ḥayl being “strength”. lam tara, jussive of raʾā, which loses its final letter. ḥiḍn, “bosom, embrace”. The shadda of الشابّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَرَجَفَ فُؤَادُهَا وَزَالَ عَقْلُهَا وَصَرَخَتْ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-rajafa fuʾāduhā wa-zāla ʿaqluhā wa-ṣarakhat ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: So-trembled her-heart and-departed her-reason, and-she-screamed a-scream great.
sentences.i: Her heart quaked, her wits left her, and she gave a great scream.
sentences.n: fuʾād, “heart”; its hamza is printed. zāla, “to pass away, be gone”. ṣarkhatan, the noun of a single act, “one scream”, as object of its own verb.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَيْقَظَ جَمِيعُ جَوَارِيهَا وَالدَّايَاتُ وَالْقَهْرَمَانَاتُ وَدَخَلْنَ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-istayqaẓa jamīʿu jawārīhā wa-al-dāyātu wa-al-qahramānātu wa-dakhalna ʿalayhā
sentences.l: So-woke all (of) her-slave-girls and-the-nurses and-the-stewardesses, and-they(f.)-came-in upon-her.
sentences.i: All her slave girls woke, and the nurses and the stewardesses, and they came in to her.
sentences.n: jawārī, “slave girls, maids”, plural of jāriya. dāya, “nurse”, the women who had reared her. qahramāna, a word of Persian origin, “stewardess, housekeeper”, a woman set over a great household. dakhalna, feminine plural, “they (women) came in”.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَيْهَا كَبِيرَتُهُنَّ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا يَاسَيِّدَتِي مَا الَّذِي أَصَابَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddamat ilayhā kabīratuhunna wa-qālat lahā yā sayyidatī mā alladhī aṣābaki
sentences.l: And-came-forward to-her their(f.)-eldest and-said to-her: O-my-lady, what (is) that-which has-struck-you?
sentences.i: The eldest of them came up to her and said, “My lady, what has come over you?”
sentences.n: kabīratuhunna, “their eldest”, the senior woman among them. The print runs yā into sayyidatī, ياسيدتي; the spacing is kept. aṣāba, Form IV, “to befall, strike”; -ki, “you”, feminine.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهَا أَيَّتُهَا الْعَجُوزُ النَّحْسُ أَيْنَ مَعْشُوقِي الشَّابُّ الْمَلِيحُ الَّذِي كَانَ نَائِمًا هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ فِي حِضْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahā ayyatuhā al-ʿajūzu al-naḥsu ayna maʿshūqī al-shābbu al-malīḥu alladhī kāna nāʾiman hādhihi al-laylata fī ḥiḍnī
sentences.l: And-she-said to-her: O you the-old-woman the-ill-omen, where (is) my-beloved, the-youth the-handsome, who was sleeping this the-night in my-bosom?
sentences.i: She said to her, “You ill-omened old woman, where is my beloved, the handsome youth who was sleeping in my arms tonight?
sentences.n: The print has الملح, a misprint for المليح, “the handsome”, corrected here: Budūr repeats the phrase a few lines on, printed in full. naḥs, “ill luck”, a noun set after al-ʿajūz as an epithet: “the old woman of ill omen”. maʿshūq, “beloved”, passive participle of ʿashiqa. hādhihi al-laylata, accusative of time, “this night”. The hamza of نائما is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبِرِينِي أَيْنَ رَاحَ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbirīnī ayna rāḥa
sentences.l: So-tell-me where he-went.
sentences.i: Tell me where he has gone.”
sentences.n: akhbirīnī, Form IV imperative, feminine, with -nī, “me”. rāḥa, “to go”, in the text’s colloquial sense; in Classical Arabic it is “to go in the evening”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مِنْهَا الْقَهْرَمَانَةُ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهَا ظَلَامًا وَخَافَتْ مِنْ بَأْسِهَا خَوْفًا عَظِيمًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat minhā al-qahramānatu hādhā al-kalāma ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihā ẓalāman wa-khāfat min baʾsihā khawfan ʿaẓīman
sentences.l: And-when heard from-her the-stewardess this the-speech, became the-light in her-face darkness, and-she-feared from her-might a-fear great.
sentences.i: When the stewardess heard these words from her, the light in her face turned to darkness, and she was sorely afraid of her anger.
sentences.n: ṣāra … ẓalāman, “became darkness”: ṣāra takes its predicate in the accusative. baʾs, “might, fury”, is printed without its hamza, باسها, a usual spelling of the text: baʾsihā. khawfan ʿaẓīman, the verb’s own noun as object, to strengthen it.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ يَاسِتِّي بُدُورُ أَيُّ شَيْءٍ هٰذَا الْكَلَامُ الْقَبِيحُ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat yā sittī Budūru ayyu shayʾin hādhā al-kalāmu al-qabīḥu
sentences.l: And-she-said: O-my-lady Budūr, what thing (is) this the-speech the-ugly?
sentences.i: and said, “Lady Budūr, what are these ugly words?”
sentences.n: sitt, “lady”, the everyday word beside sayyida; the print runs yā into it, ياستي, and the spacing is kept. ayyu shayʾin, “what thing?”, the colloquial “what?”; the shadda of ايّ and the hamza of شيء are printed. qabīḥ, “ugly, shameful”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ السِّتُّ بُدُورُ وَيْلَكِ يَا عَجُوزَ النَّحْسِ أَيْنَ مَعْشُوقِي الشَّابُّ الْمَلِيحُ صَاحِبُ الْوَجْهِ الصَّبِيحِ وَالْقَدِّ الرَّجِيحِ وَالْعُيُونِ السُّودِ وَالْحَوَاجِبِ الْمَقْرُونَةِ الَّذِي كَانَ بَائِتًا عِنْدِي فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ مِنَ الْعِشَاءِ إِلَى قُرْبِ طُلُوعِ الْفَجْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-sittu Budūru waylaki yā ʿajūza al-naḥsi ayna maʿshūqī al-shābbu al-malīḥu ṣāḥibu al-wajhi al-ṣabīḥi wa-al-qaddi al-rajīḥi wa-al-ʿuyūni al-sūdi wa-al-ḥawājibi al-maqrūnati alladhī kāna bāʾitan ʿindī fī hādhihi al-laylati mina al-ʿishāʾi ilā qurbi ṭulūʿi al-fajri
sentences.l: And-said the-lady Budūr: Woe-to-you, O old-woman (of) the-ill-omen! Where (is) my-beloved, the-youth the-handsome, owner (of) the-face the-bright and-the-stature the-outweighing and-the-eyes the-black and-the-eyebrows the-joined, who was spending-the-night with-me in this the-night from the-nightfall to (the) nearness (of the) rising (of) the-dawn?
sentences.i: The lady Budūr said, “Woe to you, you old woman of ill omen! Where is my beloved, the handsome youth with the bright face and the noble form, the black eyes and the brows that meet, who spent this night with me from nightfall until close on daybreak?”
sentences.n: The print has البست, a misprint for الست, “the lady”, corrected here. waylaki, “woe to you”, with the feminine suffix. yā ʿajūza al-naḥsi, “O old woman of ill omen”: the insult from before, now as a construct, and a noun in construct after yā is accusative. ṣabīḥ, “bright, fair”, and rajīḥ, “weighty, outweighing”, rhyme: a qadd, “stature, figure”, that outweighs all others. Brows that meet above the nose were counted a beauty. bāʾit, participle of bāta, “to spend the night”; its hamza is printed. ʿishāʾ, nightfall, the hour of the last prayer of the day.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ مَا رَأَيْتُ شَابًّا وَلَا غَيْرَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-Allāhi mā raʾaytu shābban wa-lā ghayrahu
sentences.l: And-she-said: By-God, not I-saw a-youth and-not other-than-him.
sentences.i: She said, “By God, I have seen no youth, nor anyone else.
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”, wa- of the oath. mā with the perfect denies the past. The hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَبِاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدَتِي لَا تَمْزَحِي هٰذَا الْمِزَاحَ الْخَارِجَ عَنِ الْحَدِّ فَتَرُوحَ أَرْوَاحُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-bi-Allāhi yā sayyidatī lā tamzaḥī hādhā al-mizāḥa al-khārija ʿani al-ḥaddi fa-tarūḥa arwāḥunā
sentences.l: So-by-God, O-my-lady, do-not jest this the-jesting the-going-out from the-limit, so-that-go our-souls.
sentences.i: For God’s sake, my lady, do not carry this jest so far beyond the bounds, or it will cost us our lives;
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi, “by God”, bi- of entreaty. lā tamzaḥī, feminine prohibition; mazaḥa takes its own noun, mizāḥ, as object. fa-tarūḥa, subjunctive after fa- following a prohibition: “and so our souls go”, that is, “lest our lives be lost”. tarūḥa and arwāḥ play on one root, r-w-ḥ.

sentences.t: وَرُبَّمَا يَبْلُغُ أَبَاكِ هٰذَا الْمِزَاحُ فَمَنْ كَانَ يُخَلِّصُنَا مِنْ يَدِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-rubbamā yablughu abāki hādhā al-mizāḥu fa-man kāna yukhalliṣunā min yadihi
sentences.l: And-perhaps reaches your-father this the-jesting; then-who was saving-us from his-hand?
sentences.i: and if this jest should reach your father, who would there be to save us from his hand?”
sentences.n: rubbamā, “perhaps”; its shadda is printed. balagha, “to reach”, takes the person reached as its direct object: abāki, accusative of ab, “father”, with its long ā. man kāna yukhalliṣunā, “who would be saving us”, kāna with the imperfect for what would follow. khallaṣa min, Form II, “to rescue from”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
